evidence: Read the whole section (Protecting Yourself from Hypnotists) with the draft in its second paragraph, then DRAFT, SOURCE and the_change. Words judged: “There are a lot of ways to influence people without engaging their conscious mind.” and “The Federal Trade Commission has a report on “dark patterns” - designs that trick or manipulate consumers.”, either side of his kept “Marketers and interface designers know this perfectly well.” Does what the_change says: Emulate's first and third sentences are in around his second, and his phrase “designs that trick or manipulate consumers” is back word for word (no “their”, “used to” or “trick and manipulate” in the FTC sentence). Meaning kept: the old “Even when not actively engaging the conscious mind, there are many ways to influence people” is now influence that does not involve the conscious mind, which is also his published “Influence doesn’t wait for the conscious mind to sign a form”; the FTC report on dark patterns is still a report on designs that trick or manipulate consumers. Two small shifts, neither a new claim: “actively” is gone (“without engaging” is no weaker than his published line), and the report's description becomes a gloss on the term (“a report” for “the report” adds nothing). The FTC and OECD facts are exactly his published ones. “their” is the people of the same sentence, and “this” in his kept sentence still points at that influence. Reads right in context: the “etc.” closing the list in the paragraph above runs naturally into “There are a lot of ways”, the voice is the plain voice of the neighbouring paragraphs, and the casual “has a report on” does not clash with his unchanged, more formal OECD sentence after it. I felt no seam, no tidy summary, no hedge or aside a stranger wrote, no first person, no invented fact. Went through T01-T29 and C01-C04 on the literal paragraph: none PRESENT. The close calls, each answered: T09/T13 (the paragraph runs claim, who does it, FTC, OECD, which is his published order; the change swaps wording, not order, and his kept second sentence is a real aside); T19 (the opener is a claim the next three sentences back up, and the list above never mentions the conscious mind, so it is not a bare announcement); T25 (the spaced hyphen opens an appositive gloss of a term, a real grammatical relation, not a drama colon); T26 (the S15 draft in the same context uses the same spaced hyphen a paragraph later for a different job; that is punctuation, not a repeated phrase); T15 (the structure changed, not just the words); C04 (matches his published FTC line). Linter: D9 follows the source order, accepted: a sentence-for-sentence swap makes agreement 1.00 automatic, the order is the argument's own (claim, who knows, two authorities), not a slot list, and his kept sentence is the noticing T13 asks for. E186 “without engaging their conscious mind”, accepted: the phrase is the paragraph's point and the same idea as his published line; what happens instead is answered in the section (the list above ends music, marketing ... trauma, beauty, etc., and the next three sentences name marketers and designers, the FTC's dark patterns and the OECD's steer, deceive, coerce); a positive rewording such as “go around the conscious mind” or “through the unconscious” would add a mechanism he did not state. One thing I could not check with the files I was allowed: whether Joel himself uses a spaced hyphen as a dash elsewhere in the article. It is Emulate's punctuation (S15 has it too) and it is not an AI tell (it is not an em dash), and the strict Emulate check against his own texts is where to confirm it.
